topics.title: Declarations: var, let, const, function, class
topics.summary: Every way to declare a name in JavaScript, with scope, hoisting and redeclaration rules side by side.
topics.description:
Use this page when you need to recall **exactly** how a declaration behaves. JavaScript has six declaration forms and they differ in scope, hoisting, and whether you may reassign or redeclare them.

### Forms at a glance

| Form | Scope | Hoisted as | Redeclare? | Reassign? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `var x = 1` | function (or global) | `undefined` | yes | yes |
| `let x = 1` | block | TDZ (error before line) | no | yes |
| `const x = 1` | block | TDZ | no | **no** (binding only) |
| `function f(){}` | function / block | fully hoisted | yes | yes |
| `class C {}` | block | TDZ | no | yes (binding is like `let`) |
| `import x from 'm'` | module | hoisted, live binding | no | **no** |

### Syntax variations
- Multiple declarators: `let a = 1, b = 2, c;`
- Destructuring declarators: `const { a, b: renamed = 5 } = obj;` and `const [x, , z] = arr;`
- `const` requires an initializer; `let x;` gives `undefined`.
- Loop heads: `for (let i = 0; ...)` creates a **fresh binding per iteration**; `for (const k of list)` and `for (const k in obj)` are allowed.
- Global `var`/function declarations become properties of `globalThis` in scripts; `let`/`const`/`class` do not.

### Rules worth memorising
1. `const` freezes the **binding**, not the value: `const a = []; a.push(1)` works.
2. Using a `let`/`const`/`class` name before its line throws `ReferenceError` (the temporal dead zone).
3. Assigning to an undeclared name creates a global in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode.
4. Prefer `const` by default, `let` when you must reassign, and avoid `var` in new code.
keyPoints: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let/const/class are block-scoped with a TDZ.
const prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the object.
Function declarations are hoisted completely; function expressions are not.
let in a for-loop head creates a new binding per iteration.
Top-level let/const/class do not become properties of globalThis.
pitfalls: Redeclaring with let in the same scope is a SyntaxError even if the first one was var.
typeof on a TDZ variable throws, unlike typeof on an undeclared name.
Function declarations inside blocks behave differently in sloppy vs strict mode.

examples.title: Scope, TDZ and const behaviour
examples.explanation: Shows hoisting differences and const mutation.

interview.q: What does const really guarantee?
interview.a: That the binding cannot be reassigned. The object or array it points to can still be mutated unless frozen.

interview.q: Are let and const hoisted?
interview.a: Yes, but they stay in the temporal dead zone until the declaration line runs, so early access throws a ReferenceError.

topics.title: Literal Forms: numbers, strings, templates, regex, arrays, objects
topics.summary: A reference of every literal syntax: number bases, separators, BigInt, string escapes, templates, regex, array holes and object shorthand.
topics.description:
A **literal** writes a value directly in source code. Knowing every form saves you from reaching for constructors.

### Numbers and BigInt
| Literal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `255`, `0.5`, `.5`, `5.` | decimal |
| `1e3`, `2.5E-3` | exponent notation |
| `0xFF`, `0o17`, `0b1010` | hex, octal, binary |
| `1_000_000` | numeric separator (readability only) |
| `123n`, `0xFFn` | BigInt (arbitrary precision integer) |
| `Infinity`, `NaN` | global numeric values |

### Strings
- Quotes: `'a'`, `"a"` (identical) and backticks for templates.
- Escapes: `\n \t \\ \' \" \0 \xA9 \u00A9 \u{1F600}`.
- Template literals: `` `Hi ${name}` `` can span lines and nest expressions.
- `String.raw` keeps backslashes untouched.

### Regular expressions
`/pattern/flags` with flags `d g i m s u v y`. The literal is compiled once per evaluation of the surrounding code.

### Arrays
`[1, 2, 3]`, holes `[1, , 3]` (sparse), trailing commas allowed, spread `[...a, ...b]`.

### Objects
- Shorthand: `{ x, y }`, methods: `{ greet() {} }`.
- Computed keys: `{ [key + 'Id']: 1 }`.
- Getters/setters: `{ get n() {}, set n(v) {} }`.
- Spread: `{ ...base, extra: 1 }`.
- Numeric keys become strings; `__proto__: obj` in a literal sets the prototype.

### Other
`true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined` (a global read-only property, not a keyword), and function/class expressions.
keyPoints: Use 0x, 0o, 0b prefixes and _ separators for readable numbers.
BigInt literals end with n and cannot be mixed with Number in arithmetic.
Template literals support multi-line text and ${} expressions.
Array holes create sparse arrays that skip some iteration methods.
Object literals support shorthand, computed keys, accessors and spread.
pitfalls: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 because numbers are IEEE 754 doubles.
A legacy octal like 010 is 8 in sloppy mode and a SyntaxError in strict mode.
Calling a method directly on an integer literal needs care: 5..toString() or (5).toString().

examples.title: Literal tour

interview.q: What is the difference between '', "" and backticks?
interview.a: Single and double quotes are the same; backticks create template literals with interpolation and multi-line support.

interview.q: Why use numeric separators?
interview.a: 1_000_000 is only a readability aid; the value is identical to 1000000.

topics.title: Operators: Full Table with Precedence and Associativity
topics.summary: Every operator group ordered from highest to lowest precedence, with associativity and surprising cases.
topics.description:
Precedence decides which operator binds first; **associativity** decides the order among equals. When in doubt, add parentheses.

### Table (high to low)
| Level | Operators | Assoc. |
|---|---|---|
| 17 | `( )` grouping, member `a.b`, `a[b]`, call `f()`, `new X()`, `?.` | left |
| 15 | postfix `x++ x--` | n/a |
| 14 | prefix `! ~ + - ++ -- typeof void delete await` | right |
| 13 | `**` exponent | **right** |
| 12 | `* / %` | left |
| 11 | `+ -` | left |
| 10 | `<< >> >>>` | left |
| 9 | `< <= > >= in instanceof` | left |
| 8 | `== != === !==` | left |
| 7-5 | `&` then `^` then `\|` | left |
| 4 | `&&` | left |
| 3 | `\|\|` and `??` | left |
| 2 | `? :` ternary, `=` and all compound assignment, `=>`, `yield` | right |
| 1 | `,` comma | left |

### Important notes
- `**` is right-associative: `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9 = 512`.
- You cannot write `-2 ** 2`; use `(-2) ** 2` or `-(2 ** 2)`.
- `??` cannot be mixed with `&&` or `||` without parentheses.
- `typeof x + 1` is `(typeof x) + 1`.
- Comparison chains do not work: `1 < 2 < 3` is `(true) < 3`.
- Assignment returns the assigned value, so `a = b = 0` works.
- `new Foo` without parentheses has lower precedence than `new Foo()` member calls.
- Logical assignment: `&&=`, `||=`, `??=` short-circuit and only assign when needed.
keyPoints: Exponent ** and assignment/ternary are right-associative; most others are left.
Mixing ?? with && or || requires parentheses.
Unary operators bind tighter than binary ones, except that -a ** b is a SyntaxError.
Comma operator evaluates all operands and returns the last.
Use parentheses instead of memorising low levels.
pitfalls: 1 < 2 < 3 is true but 3 > 2 > 1 is false (true > 1 is false).
a + b * c is not (a + b) * c; mixing string + number concatenates left to right.

examples.title: Precedence puzzles

interview.q: Which common operator is right-associative?
interview.a: The exponent operator, the ternary and all assignment operators.

interview.q: Why does 3 > 2 > 1 return false?
interview.a: It parses as (3 > 2) > 1, i.e. true > 1, which is 1 > 1 and false.

topics.title: Destructuring Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: All destructuring patterns for arrays, objects, parameters, loops and swaps in one place.
topics.description:
Destructuring unpacks values into variables using a pattern that mirrors the shape of the data. It works in declarations, assignments, function parameters, `for...of` heads and `catch` clauses.

### Pattern forms
| Goal | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Array positions | `const [a, b] = arr` |
| Skip items | `const [a, , c] = arr` |
| Default | `const [a = 1] = []` |
| Rest | `const [first, ...rest] = arr` |
| Object keys | `const { x, y } = obj` |
| Rename | `const { x: px } = obj` |
| Default | `const { x = 0 } = obj` |
| Rename + default | `const { x: px = 0 } = obj` |
| Computed key | `const { [k]: v } = obj` |
| Nested | `const { a: { b: [c] } } = obj` |
| Object rest | `const { x, ...others } = obj` |
| Assign to existing | `({ x, y } = obj);` (parentheses needed) |
| Swap | `[a, b] = [b, a]` |
| Parameters | `function f({ id, tags = [] } = {}) {}` |
| Loops | `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(o))` |
| Catch | `catch ({ message })` |

### Behaviour details
- Defaults apply only when the value is `undefined`, not `null`.
- Array patterns work on **any iterable** (strings, Sets, Maps, generators).
- Object patterns on `null` or `undefined` throw a TypeError.
- Primitive values are boxed: `const { length } = 'hello'` is 5.
- Defaults are evaluated lazily and may refer to earlier variables.
- A parameter default `= {}` prevents the crash when the argument is missing.
keyPoints: Array patterns use position; object patterns use property names.
Defaults trigger only for undefined.
Rest element must be last and collects the remainder.
Wrap object destructuring assignment in parentheses.
Works for any iterable on the array side.
pitfalls: Destructuring null or undefined throws a TypeError.
Forgetting the = {} default makes f() crash when f destructures its parameter.
A statement starting with { is parsed as a block, hence the leading parentheses.

examples.title: Every pattern once

interview.q: When does a default value apply in destructuring?
interview.a: Only when the extracted value is strictly undefined; null and other falsy values are kept.

interview.q: How do you swap two variables without a temp?
interview.a: Use array destructuring assignment: [a, b] = [b, a].

topics.title: Spread and Rest in Every Position
topics.summary: The same three dots do opposite jobs: spread expands, rest collects. See each place they can appear.
topics.description:
`...` means **spread** when it expands a value and **rest** when it collects values. The position tells you which.

### Spread (expanding)
| Where | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Array literal | `[...a, ...b]` | any iterable |
| Function call | `Math.max(...nums)` | very large arrays may overflow the stack |
| `new` call | `new Date(...parts)` | |
| Object literal | `{ ...a, ...b }` | own enumerable props, later wins |
| String | `[...'héllo']` | splits by code point |
| Set/Map | `[...new Set(a)]` | dedupe, convert |

### Rest (collecting)
| Where | Example |
|---|---|
| Function params | `function f(first, ...others)` |
| Array destructuring | `const [h, ...t] = arr` |
| Object destructuring | `const { id, ...data } = obj` |

### Rules
1. A rest element must be **last**, and only one is allowed.
2. Rest parameters are real arrays (unlike `arguments`).
3. Object spread is a **shallow** copy and skips non-enumerable and prototype properties.
4. Spreading `null` or `undefined` into an object is fine (nothing added); spreading them into an array throws.
5. Spreading a plain object into an array throws because it is not iterable.
6. Getters on spread objects are read once; the copy holds plain values.
7. `Object.assign` and object spread are similar, but spread defines properties while `assign` calls setters.
keyPoints: Spread expands iterables or objects; rest gathers remaining items.
Rest must be the last parameter or element.
Object spread copies own enumerable properties shallowly.
Later spread entries override earlier keys.
Rest parameters replace the old arguments object.
pitfalls: Shallow copying: nested objects stay shared after { ...obj } or [...arr].
Math.max(...hugeArray) can hit the maximum call stack or argument limit.
Spreading an object with [...obj] throws because plain objects are not iterable.

examples.title: Spread and rest together

interview.q: Difference between spread and rest?
interview.a: Spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements; rest collects remaining elements into an array or object.

interview.q: Is spread a deep copy?
interview.a: No, it only copies one level; nested references are shared.

topics.title: Function Forms Reference
topics.summary: Declaration, expression, arrow, method, accessor, generator, async, async generator, IIFE and new Function side by side.
topics.description:
JavaScript has many ways to create a function. They differ in hoisting, `this`, `arguments`, `new` ability and special behaviour.

| Form | Syntax | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Declaration | `function f(a) {}` | hoisted, has own `this` |
| Expression | `const f = function (a) {}` | not hoisted, may be named |
| Arrow | `const f = (a) => a * 2` | lexical `this`, no `arguments`, not constructable |
| Object method | `{ f(a) {} }` | has `super`, not constructable |
| Getter/setter | `{ get x() {}, set x(v) {} }` | accessor properties |
| Generator | `function* g() { yield 1 }` | returns an iterator |
| Async | `async function f() {}` | always returns a Promise |
| Async arrow | `async (a) => await a` | |
| Async generator | `async function* g() { yield 1 }` | use `for await` |
| IIFE | `(function () {})()` or `(() => {})()` | runs immediately |
| Constructor | `new Function('a', 'b', 'return a+b')` | global scope only, avoid |
| Class | `class A { constructor() {} }` | must use `new` |

### Parameter syntax
- Defaults: `(a, b = a + 1)`; rest: `(...args)`; destructured: `({ x }, [y])`.
- Trailing commas are allowed in parameter lists and calls.
- `fn.length` counts parameters **before** the first default or rest.

### Return and arrow shortcuts
- Arrow with expression body returns implicitly; to return an object literal wrap it: `() => ({ ok: true })`.
- A function without `return` returns `undefined`.
- Methods can be named with computed keys: `{ [`on${name}`]() {} }`.

### Dynamic behaviour
`fn.call(this, ...)`, `fn.apply(this, [..])`, `fn.bind(this)`; `new.target` tells a function whether it was called with `new`.
keyPoints: Only declarations are fully hoisted; expressions and arrows are not.
Arrows capture this and cannot be used with new.
Async functions always return promises; generators return iterators.
Wrap an object literal in parentheses when returning it from an arrow.
new Function ignores local scope and is rarely a good idea.
pitfalls: Using an arrow function as an object method loses the object as this.
fn.length stops counting at the first default or rest parameter.
Forgetting the parentheses around an IIFE makes the engine see a declaration.

examples.title: Many forms in one file
examples.explanation: Each function form returns something observable.

interview.q: Which function forms can be used with new?
interview.a: Function declarations/expressions and classes; arrows, methods, generators and async functions cannot.

interview.q: What does new Function do differently?
interview.a: It compiles a string as a function body in the global scope, so it cannot see local variables, and is similar in risk to eval.

topics.title: Class Syntax Full Reference
topics.summary: Every part of class syntax: constructor, fields, private members, static members, static blocks, accessors and extends.
keyPoints: Fields are per instance; methods are shared on the prototype.
Private members start with # and are truly inaccessible outside the class body.
Static blocks run once at class definition time.
Derived constructors must call super() before using this.
Class bodies are always in strict mode.
pitfalls: Passing an unbound method as a callback loses this.
Referencing this before super() throws a ReferenceError.
Private names cannot be created dynamically or accessed with bracket notation.

examples.title: A class using most features
examples.explanation: Fields, private, static, accessor, static block.

interview.q: Are class methods enumerable?
interview.a: No, class methods are non-enumerable on the prototype, but class fields are own enumerable properties.

interview.q: What is a static initialization block for?
interview.a: Running complex setup code once when the class is defined, with access to private static members.

topics.title: Loops, break, continue and Labels
topics.summary: All loop statements plus break, continue and labeled statements, including which one to use for what.
topics.description:
### Loop forms
| Loop | Use for |
|---|---|
| `for (init; test; update) {}` | counted loops |
| `while (cond) {}` | unknown number of iterations |
| `do {} while (cond)` | run at least once |
| `for (const k in obj) {}` | enumerable **keys** (including inherited) of an object |
| `for (const v of iterable) {}` | **values** of any iterable |
| `for await (const v of asyncIterable) {}` | async iteration |
| `arr.forEach(fn)` | side effects, cannot `break` |

### Flow control
- `break` leaves the nearest loop or `switch`.
- `continue` skips to the next iteration (runs the update clause in a `for`).
- A **label** names a statement so `break`/`continue` can target an outer loop:

```js
outer: for (const row of grid) {
  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell === target) break outer;
  }
}
```

- Labels also work on plain blocks: `block: { if (x) break block; ... }`.
- `return` inside a loop in a function exits the whole function.
- `for` heads can be empty: `for (;;) {}` is an infinite loop.
- Each `let` in a `for` head gets a new binding per iteration, so closures capture the right value.

### Choosing
- Arrays: prefer `for...of` or array methods.
- Objects: `Object.entries(obj)` with `for...of`; avoid `for...in` on arrays.
- Need an index with `for...of`: `for (const [i, v] of arr.entries())`.
- `forEach`, `map`, `filter` do not await; use `for...of` with `await` for sequential async work.
keyPoints: for...of iterates values of iterables; for...in iterates enumerable keys of objects.
Labels let break and continue target outer loops.
do...while always runs its body once.
Use for...of with await for sequential async loops.
let in the loop head is re-created each iteration.
pitfalls: for...in on an array yields string indices and inherited enumerable props.
Array.forEach ignores await and cannot be stopped with break.
Modifying a collection while iterating it can skip or repeat items.

examples.title: Labels and loop styles
examples.explanation: Find a value in a grid and compare for-in with for-of.

interview.q: Difference between for...in and for...of?
interview.a: for...in loops over enumerable property names (strings), including inherited ones; for...of loops over values produced by an iterable's iterator.

interview.q: How do you break out of nested loops?
interview.a: Use a labeled break (break outer) or move the loops into a function and return.

topics.title: switch, try/catch/finally and Error Forms
topics.summary: Syntax and edge cases of switch (fall-through, scope, strict compare) and try/catch/finally including optional catch binding.
topics.description:
### switch
```js
switch (expr) {
  case 1:
  case 2:            // grouped cases (intentional fall-through)
    doSomething();
    break;
  case 3: {          // braces give the case its own block scope
    const local = 1;
    break;
  }
  default:           // may appear anywhere, runs if nothing matches
    fallback();
}
```
- Comparison uses **strict equality** (`===`).
- Without `break`, execution **falls through** into the next case.
- All cases share one block scope unless you add braces, so two `let x` in different cases clash.
- `switch (true) { case x > 5: ... }` is a pattern for range checks.

### try / catch / finally
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `try {} catch (e) {}` | handle error |
| `try {} catch {}` | optional catch binding, no variable |
| `try {} finally {}` | cleanup, error still propagates |
| `try {} catch (e) {} finally {}` | both |
| `catch ({ name, message })` | destructured error |

### Rules
1. `finally` always runs, even after `return`, `break` or a thrown error.
2. A `return` in `finally` **overrides** returns and swallows exceptions.
3. `throw` accepts any value, but throw `Error` objects to keep stack traces.
4. `catch` only catches **synchronous** errors and rejected promises awaited inside it.
5. Rethrow what you cannot handle: `throw e`.
6. Errors can carry a cause: `throw new Error('msg', { cause: err })`.
7. Built-in types: `Error`, `TypeError`, `RangeError`, `SyntaxError`, `ReferenceError`, `EvalError`, `URIError`, `AggregateError`.
keyPoints: switch uses strict equality and falls through without break.
Wrap case bodies in braces when declaring variables.
finally always runs and can override return values.
catch without a binding is allowed.
try/catch does not catch errors thrown later in async callbacks.
pitfalls: Forgetting break creates accidental fall-through bugs.
return inside finally silently discards earlier returns and errors.
throw 'string' loses the stack trace and breaks instanceof checks.

examples.title: Switch fall-through and finally
examples.explanation: Shows grouping, braces and the finally override.

interview.q: What does finally do when try has a return?
interview.a: finally still runs before the function returns; if finally itself returns, that value replaces the earlier one.

interview.q: Does switch use == or ===?
interview.a: Strict equality ===.

topics.title: Modules: import and export in All Forms
topics.summary: Complete list of ES module import and export syntaxes, plus dynamic import, import.meta and live bindings.
topics.description:
ES modules (`.mjs`, `type: module`, or `<script type="module">`) are strict, have their own scope, and execute once.

### Export forms
| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `export const a = 1; export function f(){}; export class C {}` | named, inline |
| `export { a, f as g }` | named list with rename |
| `export default expr` | one default per module |
| `export { x as default }` | default via list |
| `export * from './m.js'` | re-export all named (not default) |
| `export * as ns from './m.js'` | re-export as namespace |
| `export { a, b as c } from './m.js'` | re-export selected |
| `export { default } from './m.js'` | re-export a default |

### Import forms
| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `import x from './m.js'` | default |
| `import { a, b as c } from './m.js'` | named |
| `import x, { a } from './m.js'` | default + named |
| `import * as ns from './m.js'` | namespace object |
| `import './side-effect.js'` | run only |
| `import data from './d.json' with { type: 'json' }` | import attributes |
| `const m = await import('./m.js')` | dynamic, returns a promise |
| `import.meta.url` | URL of the current module |

### Key behaviour
- Imports are **live read-only bindings**, not copies.
- Import declarations are hoisted and must be at the top level.
- Circular imports work but may see uninitialised (TDZ) bindings.
- Module code runs once; later imports reuse the same instance.
- Browsers require file extensions and relative paths (`./`); bundlers can relax this.
- Top-level `await` is allowed in modules.
keyPoints: Named exports use the exact binding name; default exports can be imported under any name.
Imports are live, read-only views of the exporting module's variables.
Use dynamic import() for lazy loading and conditional loading.
export * does not re-export the default export.
Modules are always strict and execute once.
pitfalls: Mixing require() and import in the same file causes errors in Node unless configured.
Assigning to an imported binding throws a TypeError.
Circular dependencies can expose bindings in the TDZ.

examples.title: Module syntax reference
examples.explanation: Multi-file code shown for viewing since modules need separate files.

interview.q: Are ES module imports copies of the exported values?
interview.a: No, they are live bindings; if the exporter changes its variable, importers see the new value.

interview.q: How do you load a module lazily?
interview.a: Use dynamic import(), which returns a promise resolving to the module namespace object.

topics.title: Optional Chaining, Nullish and Logical Assignment Forms
topics.summary: All forms of ?., ??, ||, && and the three logical assignment operators with exact falsy vs nullish behaviour.
topics.description:
These operators make "safe access" and "default value" code short, but each reacts to different values.

### Optional chaining `?.`
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a?.b` | `undefined` if `a` is `null`/`undefined`, else `a.b` |
| `a?.[expr]` | safe bracket access |
| `a?.()` | call only if `a` is a function value (not null/undefined) |
| `a.b?.()` | call method only if it exists |
| `delete a?.b` | safe delete |

The whole rest of the chain is **short-circuited**: `a?.b.c.d` stops at the first `?.` that hits nullish.

### Defaults: `||` vs `??`
| Value | `v \|\| 'x'` | `v ?? 'x'` |
|---|---|---|
| `0`, `''`, `false`, `NaN` | `'x'` | keeps the value |
| `null`, `undefined` | `'x'` | `'x'` |

Use `??` when `0`, `''` or `false` are valid values.

### Logical assignment
| Operator | Equivalent | Assigns when |
|---|---|---|
| `a \|\|= b` | `a \|\| (a = b)` | `a` is falsy |
| `a &&= b` | `a && (a = b)` | `a` is truthy |
| `a ??= b` | `a ?? (a = b)` | `a` is null/undefined |

They **short-circuit**, so setters and side effects only occur when an assignment is needed.

### Rules
- `??` cannot be combined with `||`/`&&` without parentheses.
- `a?.b = 1` is a SyntaxError; optional chaining cannot be an assignment target.
- `a?.b` on a non-nullish primitive just reads normally.
- `?.` does not guard against thrown errors or against `a` being declared at all (undeclared names still throw).
keyPoints: ?. returns undefined instead of throwing for null/undefined links.
?? only replaces null and undefined; || replaces every falsy value.
??= is ideal for lazily initialising defaults and caches.
Optional chaining short-circuits the whole remaining chain.
Logical assignments only write when the condition requires it.
pitfalls: Using || for numeric or boolean defaults turns valid 0 or false into the fallback.
Overusing ?. hides genuine data bugs by silently returning undefined.
Optional call a?.() still throws if a is a non-function truthy value.

examples.title: Falsy vs nullish

interview.q: When should you use ?? over ||?
interview.a: When 0, empty string or false are legitimate values that must not be replaced by a default.

interview.q: What does a?.b.c do when a is null?
interview.a: The entire chain short-circuits and evaluates to undefined without throwing.

topics.title: Tagged Templates and String.raw
topics.summary: How a tag function receives strings and values, the raw array, caching rules, and real uses such as escaping and DSLs.
topics.description:
A **tagged template** puts a function name before a template literal: ``tag`a ${x} b` ``. The function is called with the literal parts and the interpolated values rather than a finished string.

### Signature
```js
function tag(strings, ...values) {}
```
- `strings` is an array of cooked string pieces, always **one longer** than `values`.
- `strings.raw` is the array of the same pieces with backslashes unprocessed.
- The tag can return **anything**, not just a string.
- The `strings` array is frozen and the **same object** is reused for each call site, which libraries use for caching.

### Syntax forms
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ``tag`text` `` | tag with no values |
| ``obj.method`x ${1}` `` | member function as tag |
| ``tag`a``b` `` | chained tags: second tag receives the result of the first |
| ``String.raw`C:\new` `` | built-in tag giving the raw text |
| ``new (getTag())`x` `` | tags can be any call expression |

### Typical uses
- Safe HTML or SQL escaping: wrap values, never concatenate raw input.
- Internationalisation and formatting helpers.
- Styled-component CSS-in-JS and GraphQL (`gql`) queries.
- Highlight or transform interpolated values.

### Notes
- In ES2018+ tagged templates may contain invalid escape sequences; cooked pieces become `undefined` while `raw` keeps the text.
- A tag function is called at runtime on every evaluation, but the strings array stays identical.
keyPoints: Tag receives (strings, ...values); strings.length is values.length + 1.
strings.raw gives unprocessed backslashes.
The tag can return any value type.
Great for escaping, DSLs, and CSS/SQL helpers.
The strings array is frozen and identity-stable per call site.
pitfalls: Building SQL by plain template literal is injection-prone; use a tag that parameterises.
Forgetting that strings has one more entry than values causes off-by-one bugs.

examples.title: A highlighting and an escaping tag

interview.q: What are the arguments of a tag function?
interview.a: An array of string pieces (with a raw property) followed by each interpolated value as separate arguments.

interview.q: What does String.raw do?
interview.a: It is a built-in tag that returns the template with escape sequences left unprocessed.

topics.title: Getters, Setters and Property Accessors
topics.summary: All ways to define accessor properties: object literals, classes, defineProperty, static and private accessors.
topics.description:
An **accessor property** has a getter and/or setter function instead of a stored value. Reading runs the getter; assigning runs the setter, so you can compute, validate or log.

### Where to define them
| Place | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Object literal | `{ get full() {...}, set full(v) {...} }` |
| Class | `class A { get x() {} set x(v) {} }` |
| Static | `static get instance() {}` |
| Private | `get #secret() {}` |
| Computed | `get [key]() {}` |
| Existing object | `Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', { get(){}, set(v){}, enumerable: true, configurable: true })` |
| Several at once | `Object.defineProperties(o, {...})` |
| Read descriptor | `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(o, 'x')` |

### Rules
1. A getter has **no parameters**; a setter takes **exactly one**.
2. A getter alone makes a read-only property (assignments are ignored silently in sloppy mode, throw in strict mode).
3. Accessors defined in classes live on the prototype and are non-enumerable; in literals they are own enumerable properties.
4. Accessors are inherited and can be overridden in subclasses (override both if you override one!).
5. `JSON.stringify` and spread **call getters** and store the returned value; setters are never copied.
6. Use accessors for derived values, validation and lazy computation (replace the getter with a value on first access).
7. Do not make getters slow or side-effectful; people expect property reads to be cheap.

### Lazy getter pattern
Inside the getter use `Object.defineProperty(this, 'x', { value: computed })` so subsequent reads skip the function.
keyPoints: Getters take no params; setters take exactly one.
A property with only a getter is read-only.
Class accessors are on the prototype; literal accessors are own properties.
Spread and JSON.stringify invoke getters and copy results.
Overriding a getter in a subclass without the setter removes the setter.
pitfalls: A setter that assigns to the same property name causes infinite recursion; use a different backing field such as #value or _value.
Overriding only the getter in a subclass makes the inherited setter unreachable (assignments silently do nothing).

examples.title: Validation and lazy getter
examples.explanation: Setter with a private field and a self-replacing getter.

interview.q: Does object spread copy getters?
interview.a: It reads the getter and copies the resulting value as a normal data property.

interview.q: What happens if a getter exists without a setter and you assign?
interview.a: Nothing in sloppy mode, a TypeError in strict mode.

topics.title: Symbols and Well-Known Symbols
topics.summary: Symbol creation, registry, and the well-known symbols (iterator, toPrimitive, hasInstance and more) that customise built-in behaviour.
topics.description:
A **symbol** is a unique, immutable primitive often used as a collision-free property key.

### Creating symbols
| Syntax | Notes |
|---|---|
| `Symbol('desc')` | always unique; description is only a label |
| `Symbol.for('key')` | global registry, same key returns same symbol |
| `Symbol.keyFor(sym)` | key of a registry symbol, else `undefined` |
| `sym.description` | read the label |

Symbol keys are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys`, and `JSON.stringify`; use `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` or `Reflect.ownKeys` to see them. `new Symbol()` throws.

### Well-known symbols
| Symbol | Customises |
|---|---|
| `Symbol.iterator` | `for...of`, spread, destructuring |
| `Symbol.asyncIterator` | `for await...of` |
| `Symbol.toPrimitive` | conversion to primitive (`hint`: `'number'`, `'string'`, `'default'`) |
| `Symbol.toStringTag` | the tag in `Object.prototype.toString` |
| `Symbol.hasInstance` | `instanceof` |
| `Symbol.species` | constructor used by derived array/promise methods |
| `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable` | `Array.prototype.concat` |
| `Symbol.match` / `replace` / `search` / `split` | string methods with custom objects |
| `Symbol.unscopables` | names excluded from `with` |
| `Symbol.dispose` / `asyncDispose` | `using` declarations |

### Uses
- Hidden-ish metadata on objects you do not own.
- Constants that must never clash (enum-like).
- Protocol hooks (iteration, conversion) in your own classes.

Symbols are **not truly private**; they can be discovered by reflection. Use `#private` fields for real privacy.
keyPoints: Every Symbol() call returns a unique value; Symbol.for shares through a global registry.
Symbol-keyed properties are ignored by Object.keys, for...in and JSON.
Well-known symbols are hooks that let your objects customise built-in operations.
Symbol.toPrimitive controls how an object converts in arithmetic and templates.
Symbols are not private; reflection can list them.
pitfalls: Implicit conversion of a symbol to a string throws a TypeError; use String(sym) or sym.toString().
JSON.stringify silently drops symbol values and symbol keys.

examples.title: Custom conversion, iteration and instanceof
examples.explanation: Three well-known symbols in one class.

interview.q: Are symbol properties private?
interview.a: No. They are hidden from normal enumeration but can be found with Object.getOwnPropertySymbols or Reflect.ownKeys; use #fields for privacy.

interview.q: What is Symbol.toPrimitive?
interview.a: A method that defines how an object converts to a primitive, receiving the hint 'number', 'string' or 'default'.

topics.title: Iteration Protocols: Iterable, Iterator, Generators
topics.summary: The exact contract of iterable and iterator objects, how for...of uses it, and generator and async iteration forms.
topics.description:
Two protocols power `for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, `Map`, `Set` and `Promise.all`.

### The contracts
| Protocol | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Iterable** | has a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator |
| **Iterator** | has `next()` returning `{ value, done }` |
| Optional | `return()` (called on early exit like `break`) and `throw()` |
| **Async iterable** | `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` whose `next()` returns a promise of `{ value, done }` |

### Iterables in the language
Arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`, `TypedArray`, `arguments`, NodeList, generators and the results of `entries()`, `keys()`, `values()`.
Plain objects are **not** iterable; use `Object.entries(obj)`.

### Generators (the easy way)
```js
function* gen() {
  const x = yield 1;     // value sent in via next(x)
  yield* otherIterable;  // delegate
  return 'end';          // reported as done: true (ignored by for...of)
}
```
- A generator object is both an iterator **and** iterable (it returns itself).
- `gen.return(v)` finishes it early; `gen.throw(err)` throws inside at the paused `yield`.
- `async function*` plus `for await (const x of ...)` handles streams of promises.

### Consumers
`for...of`, `[...it]`, `Array.from(it)`, `new Set(it)`, `Promise.all(it)`, `Object.fromEntries(it)`, and destructuring `[a, b] = it` all call `Symbol.iterator`.

### Iterator helpers
Modern engines add `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `toArray`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `forEach` on iterators.
keyPoints: Iterable = has Symbol.iterator; iterator = has next() returning {value, done}.
Generators implement both protocols automatically.
Breaking out of for...of calls the iterator's return() method.
Plain objects are not iterable; use entries/keys/values.
Async generators with for await handle async streams.
pitfalls: A one-shot iterator (generator) is exhausted after one pass; make a fresh one to loop again.
The return value of a generator is not visible to for...of or spread.

examples.title: Custom iterable and generator control
examples.explanation: Range class, send values, early exit.

interview.q: What is the difference between an iterable and an iterator?
interview.a: An iterable can produce an iterator through Symbol.iterator; an iterator is the object with next() that yields {value, done} results.

interview.q: What happens on break inside for...of?
interview.a: The engine calls the iterator's return() method if present, allowing cleanup.

topics.title: ASI Rules and Strict Mode
topics.summary: When JavaScript inserts semicolons for you, the dangerous lines that break, and everything that changes in strict mode.
topics.description:
### Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI)
The parser inserts a semicolon when it hits a token that cannot continue the statement **and** there is a newline before it (or `}` / end of input), or after `do...while`.

**Restricted productions** - no newline is allowed between the keyword and its operand, so a semicolon is inserted:
- `return`, `throw`, `break`, `continue`, `yield`, and postfix `++`/`--`.

```js
return
{ ok: true }   // returns undefined!
```

**Lines that start with a dangerous character** continue the previous line - ASI does NOT help:
`(`, `[`, `` ` ``, `+`, `-`, `/`. If you skip semicolons, start such lines with `;`.

### Strict mode
Enable with `'use strict'` at the top of a script or function. Modules and class bodies are strict automatically.

| Sloppy mode | Strict mode |
|---|---|
| Undeclared assignment creates a global | `ReferenceError` |
| Assigning to read-only property fails silently | `TypeError` |
| `this` in a plain function call is `globalThis` | `undefined` |
| Duplicate parameter names allowed | SyntaxError |
| Octal literal `010` allowed | SyntaxError |
| `with` statement allowed | SyntaxError |
| `delete variable` ignored | SyntaxError |
| `arguments` mirrors parameters | independent copy |
| `eval` leaks variables into scope | own scope |
| Reserved words (`let`, `static`, `implements`) usable as names | not allowed |
| Function declarations in blocks hoist weirdly | block-scoped |

Use strict mode always - modules and classes already give it to you.
keyPoints: ASI inserts semicolons at line breaks only when the parse would otherwise fail.
return, throw, break, continue and ++/-- cannot be followed by a newline.
Lines beginning with ( [ ` + - / are never auto-terminated from above.
Strict mode turns silent mistakes into errors and makes this undefined in plain calls.
ES modules and class bodies are strict by default.
pitfalls: return followed by a newline then an object literal returns undefined.
Omitting semicolons before a line that starts with ( or [ merges the two lines into one expression.

examples.title: ASI traps
examples.explanation: Demonstrates return newline and the this difference.

interview.q: Why does return followed by a newline break?
interview.a: ASI inserts a semicolon right after return, so the object on the next line is never returned.

interview.q: Name three changes strict mode makes.
interview.a: Undeclared assignments throw, this is undefined in plain function calls, and silent failures like writing to read-only properties throw TypeErrors.
